episodes.title: Why 60 FPS Can Still Stutter
episodes.thesis: A steady frame-time rhythm matters as much as the FPS counter.
frames: Sixty frames per second can still feel stuttery. The number is real — but it does not tell you when each frame arrived.
FPS is an average across time. Smoothness also lives in the gaps — the rhythm between one finished frame and the next.
At a clean sixty, a new image arrives about every sixteen point seven milliseconds. Tick — tick — tick — an even visual cadence.
Now let one frame take forty milliseconds. Faster frames can pull the average back up, yet your eye still catches that single pause.
That is uneven frame pacing. The engine, driver and display must hand frames over steadily — not merely finish sixty somewhere inside a second.
So when a game feels rough, watch the frame-time graph as well as the FPS counter. The average can hide the hitch.

episodes.title: Why Some PC Games Stutter the First Time
episodes.thesis: A game can pause while preparing a new graphics pipeline, then run that same moment smoothly from cache.
frames: Ever notice a PC game hitch the first time an effect appears, then glide through the same moment later? The scene may not be the problem.
Modern graphics APIs bundle shader choices and fixed settings into pipeline state objects. The GPU needs the right combination before it can draw.
If that pipeline is not ready, the game may compile or create it just as the effect arrives. That preparation can interrupt an otherwise steady frame.
Once cached, the same pipeline can be reused. That is why a second run may feel smoother even when the graphics settings have not changed.
Good engines pre-build likely pipelines and preserve useful caches, but the possible combinations can be huge. Driver updates may also invalidate old cache data.
Not every hitch is shader compilation. But a one-time pause tied to a new effect is a useful clue: the game may be building tomorrow's smooth frame today.

episodes.title: How Games Rebuild Detail From Previous Frames
episodes.thesis: Temporal upscalers combine a new low-resolution frame with motion-aware history rather than simply stretching one image.
frames: That sharp four-K image may not begin as four-K. Many games render fewer pixels, then rebuild detail with information gathered across time.
A temporal upscaler receives the new frame plus motion vectors, depth and samples saved from earlier frames. Each input answers a different question.
Motion vectors show where surfaces moved. Depth helps separate foreground from background. History supplies detail that one lower-resolution frame cannot hold alone.
The system then reprojects useful history into the current view and rejects information that no longer belongs. Done well, the final image looks far denser.
Fast reveals, thin geometry and particles can break that history. Old samples may linger as ghosting, or fresh pixels may shimmer before enough evidence arrives.
So temporal upscaling is not a fancy stretch. It is a moving reconstruction problem — borrowing from the past without letting the past haunt the present.

episodes.title: How Stereo Headphones Place Sounds Behind You
episodes.thesis: Spatial audio filters sound with direction-dependent head and ear cues before sending it through two headphone channels.
frames: Your headphones have only two speakers, yet a game can place footsteps behind you and above you. The trick begins before the sound reaches either ear.
A spatial audio engine treats each sound as an object with a position. It then calculates how that direction should arrive at your left and right ears.
The filter models tiny timing, level and frequency differences caused by the head and outer ear. Together, those cues are called an H-R-T-F.
Turn the camera and the filters change. The waveform in each channel shifts, while your brain interprets those changes as a sound moving through space.
People have different ears, so one generic profile will not feel equally precise for everyone. Personalised profiles can improve the match where a platform supports them.
There are still only two headphone channels at the end. The three-dimensional stage happens in the filtering — and your brain finishes the render.

episodes.title: Why Games Do Not Keep Every Texture in VRAM
episodes.thesis: Texture streaming keeps the most useful mip levels resident and moves detail as the camera and memory budget change.
frames: A modern game can contain far more texture data than your graphics memory can hold at once. The solution is not to load the whole world.
Textures are stored in mip levels: large detailed versions for close views and progressively smaller versions for distant or tiny surfaces.
The streaming system estimates which levels matter for the current camera. Useful detail moves into memory while less valuable data can be released.
That turns V-RAM into a working set rather than a warehouse. The engine keeps changing residency as you move, turn and reveal new parts of the scene.
If the detailed mip arrives late, you may briefly see a soft surface snap into focus. If the budget is too tight, sharper levels may never stay resident.
So the texture on disk is not always the texture on screen. What you see is the best level the streaming system has ready for that moment.

episodes.title: How Ray Tracing Avoids Testing Every Triangle
episodes.thesis: A bounding volume hierarchy lets rays discard large empty regions before testing nearby geometry.
frames: Ray tracing sounds impossible at game speed. A single ray could meet millions of triangles — unless the renderer learns where not to look.
Common real-time ray-tracing systems organise geometry into a bounding volume hierarchy, or B-V-H. Think of nested boxes around smaller groups of shapes.
A ray first tests a large box. If it misses, every triangle inside that branch is rejected at once. Only promising branches are opened further.
The search narrows from world-sized regions to smaller boxes, then finally to the few triangles that might actually be hit. Empty space becomes cheap.
Building and updating that structure still costs time, especially when geometry moves. Engines balance rebuild quality, update cost and how many rays they can afford.
So real-time ray tracing does not brute-force the whole scene. It wins by asking a better first question: which parts can this ray ignore?

episodes.title: Why More FPS Does Not Always Mean Faster Input
episodes.thesis: Input latency depends on how long work waits across the CPU, render queue, GPU and display, not only the final frame rate.
frames: A high frame rate can still feel slightly behind your hands. The missing number is not frames per second — it is how long your newest input waits.
The CPU prepares rendering work and the GPU executes it. To keep the GPU busy, a system may queue more than one frame ahead.
That queue can improve utilisation, but an input sampled now may sit behind older prepared frames. The counter stays high while the response arrives later.
Latency controls reduce that waiting by synchronising CPU work more closely with GPU capacity. A sensible frame cap can also prevent a deep queue in some workloads.
The result depends on the bottleneck. If the game is not GPU-bound, or another stage dominates, the same setting may produce a smaller change.
So judge responsiveness across the whole path: input, simulation, render queue, GPU and display. The fastest counter is not automatically the freshest frame.
